# Authenticate requests with the Bot Connector API - Bot Service | Microsoft Learn

Your bot communicates with the Bot Connector service using HTTP over a secured channel (SSL/TLS). When your bot sends a request to the Connector service, it must include information that the Connector service can use to verify its identity. Likewise, when the Connector service sends a request to your bot, it must include information that the bot can use to verify its identity. This article describes the authentication technologies and requirements for the service-level authentication that takes place between a bot and the Bot Connector service. If you're writing your own authentication code, you must implement the security procedures described in this article to enable your bot to exchange messages with the Bot Connector service.

Important

If you're writing your own authentication code, it's critical that you implement all security procedures correctly. By implementing all steps in this article, you can mitigate the risk of an attacker being able to read messages that are sent to your bot, send messages that impersonate your bot, and steal secret keys.

If you're using the [Bot Framework SDK](../index-bf-sdk), you don't need to implement the security procedures described in this article, because the SDK automatically does it for you. Simply configure your project with the App ID and password that you obtained for your bot during [registration](../bot-service-quickstart-registration) and the SDK will handle the rest.

## Authentication technologies

Four authentication technologies are used to establish trust between a bot and the Bot Connector:

| Technology | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **SSL/TLS** | SSL/TLS is used for all service-to-service connections. `X.509v3` certificates are used to establish the identity of all HTTPS services. **Clients should always inspect service certificates to ensure they are trusted and valid.** (Client certificates are NOT used as part of this scheme.) |
| **OAuth 2.0** | OAuth 2.0 uses the Microsoft Entra ID account login service to generate a secure token that a bot can use to send messages. This token is a service-to-service token; no user login is required. |
| **JSON Web Token (JWT)** | JSON Web Tokens are used to encode tokens that are sent to and from the bot. **Clients should fully verify all JWT tokens that they receive**, according to the requirements outlined in this article. |
| **OpenID metadata** | The Bot Connector service publishes a list of valid tokens that it uses to sign its own JWT tokens to OpenID metadata at a well-known, static endpoint. |

This article describes how to use these technologies via standard HTTPS and JSON. No special SDKs are required, although you may find that helpers for OpenID and others are useful.

## Authenticate requests from your bot to the Bot Connector service

To communicate with the Bot Connector service, you must specify an access token in the `Authorization` header of each API request, using this format:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

To get and use a JWT token for your bot:

1. Your bot sends a GET HTTP request to the MSA Login Service.
2. The response from the service contains the JWT token to use.
3. Your bot includes this JWT token in the authorization header in requests to the Bot Connector service.

### Step 1: Request an access token from the Microsoft Entra ID account login service

Important

If you haven't already done so, you must [register your bot](../bot-service-quickstart-registration) with the Bot Framework to obtain its AppID and password. You need the bot's App ID and password to request an access token.

Your bot identity can be managed in Azure in a few different ways.

- As a *user-assigned managed identity*, so that you don't need to manage the bot's credentials yourself.
- As a *single-tenant* app.
- As a *multi-tenant* app.

Request an access token based on your bot's application type.

# [Multi-tenant](#tab/multitenant)
To request an access token from the login service, issue the following request, replacing **MICROSOFT-APP-ID** and **MICROSOFT-APP-PASSWORD** with the bot's AppID and password that you obtained when you [registered](../bot-service-quickstart-registration) your bot with the Bot Service.

```http
POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/botframework.com/oauth2/v2.0/token
Host: login.microsoftonline.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=MICROSOFT-APP-ID&client_secret=REDACTED&scope=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.botframework.com%2F.default
```

# [Single-tenant](#tab/singletenant)
To request an access token from the login service, issue the following request, replacing **MICROSOFT-APP-ID**, **MICROSOFT-APP-PASSWORD** and **MICROSOFT-TENANT-ID** with the bot's AppID, password and tenant Id that you obtained when you [registered](../bot-service-quickstart-registration) your bot with the Bot Service.

```http
POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/MICROSOFT-TENANT-ID/oauth2/v2.0/token
Host: login.microsoftonline.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=MICROSOFT-APP-ID&client_secret=REDACTED&scope=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.botframework.com%2F.default
```

# [User-assigned managed identity](#tab/userassigned)
App Service and Azure Functions provide an internally accessible REST endpoint for token retrieval. To request an access token from the `MSI/token` endpoint, make a GET request to the endpoint. Use the `resource` and `client_id` query parameters. Set `resource` to `https://api.botframework.com` and `client_id` to the bot's managed identity app ID. The request doesn't require other query parameters.

- For more information about the token endpoint, see [Connect to Azure services in app code](/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-managed-identity?context=%2Fazure%2Factive-directory%2Fmanaged-identities-azure-resources%2Fcontext%2Fmsi-context&tabs=portal%2Chttp#connect-to-azure-services-in-app-code).
- For more information about bot app IDs, see [Create an Azure Bot resource](../bot-service-quickstart-registration).

---

### Step 2: Obtain the JWT token from the Microsoft Entra ID account login service response

If your application is authorized by the login service, the JSON response body will specify your access token, its type, and its expiration (in seconds).

When adding the token to the `Authorization` header of a request, you must use the exact value that is specified in this response—don't escape or encode the token value. The access token is valid until its expiration. To prevent token expiration from impacting your bot's performance, you may choose to cache and proactively refresh the token.

This example shows a response from the Microsoft Entra ID account login service:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
... (other headers)
```

```json
{
    "token_type":"Bearer",
    "expires_in":3600,
    "ext_expires_in":3600,
    "access_token":"REDACTED"
}
```

### Step 3: Specify the JWT token in the Authorization header of requests

When you send an API request to the Bot Connector service, specify the access token in the `Authorization` header of the request using this format:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

All requests that you send to the Bot Connector service must include the access token in the `Authorization` header. If the token is correctly formed, isn't expired, and was generated by the Microsoft Entra ID account login service, the Bot Connector service will authorize the request. Additional checks are performed to ensure that the token belongs to the bot that sent the request.

The following example shows how to specify the access token in the `Authorization` header of the request.

```http
POST https://smba.trafficmanager.net/teams/v3/conversations/12345/activities
Authorization: Bearer REDACTED

(JSON-serialized Activity message goes here)
```

Important

Only specify the JWT token in the `Authorization` header of requests you send to the Bot Connector service. Do NOT send the token over unsecured channels and do NOT include it in HTTP requests that you send to other services. The JWT token that you obtain from the the Microsoft Entra ID account login service is like a password and should be handled with great care. Anyone that possesses the token may use it to perform operations on behalf of your bot.

#### Bot to Connector: example JWT components

```json
header:
{
  typ: "JWT",
  alg: "RS256",
  x5t: "<SIGNING KEY ID>",
  kid: "<SIGNING KEY ID>"
},
payload:
{
  aud: "https://api.botframework.com",
  iss: "https://sts.windows.net/d6d49420-f39b-4df7-a1dc-d59a935871db/",
  nbf: 1481049243,
  exp: 1481053143,
  appid: "<YOUR MICROSOFT APP ID>",
  ... other fields follow
}
```

Note

Actual fields may vary in practice. Create and validate all JWT tokens as specified above.

## Authenticate requests from the Bot Connector service to your bot

When the Bot Connector service sends a request to your bot, it specifies a signed JWT token in the `Authorization` header of the request. Your bot can authenticate calls from the Bot Connector service by verifying the authenticity of the signed JWT token.

To authenticate calls from the Bot Connector service:

1. Your bot gets the JWT token from the authorization header in requests sent from the Bot Connector service.
2. Your bot gets the OpenID metadata document for the Bot Connector service.
3. Your bot gets the list of valid signing keys from the document.
4. Your bot verifies the authenticity of the JWT token.

### Step 2: Get the OpenID metadata document

The OpenID metadata document specifies the location of a second document that lists the Bot Connector service's valid signing keys. To get the OpenID metadata document, issue this request via HTTPS:

```http
GET https://login.botframework.com/v1/.well-known/openidconfiguration
```

Tip

This is a static URL that you can hardcode into your application.

The following example shows an OpenID metadata document that is returned in response to the `GET` request. The `jwks_uri` property specifies the location of the document that contains the Bot Connector service's valid signing keys.

```json
{
    "issuer": "https://api.botframework.com",
    "authorization_endpoint": "https://invalid.botframework.com",
    "jwks_uri": "https://login.botframework.com/v1/.well-known/keys",
    "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": [
      "RS256"
    ],
    "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [
      "private_key_jwt"
    ]
}
```

### Step 3: Get the list of valid signing keys

To get the list of valid signing keys, issue a `GET` request via HTTPS to the URL specified by the `jwks_uri` property in the OpenID metadata document. For example:

```http
GET https://login.botframework.com/v1/.well-known/keys
```

The response body specifies the document in the [JWK format](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7517) but also includes an additional property for each key: `endorsements`.

Tip

The list of keys is stable and may be cached, but new keys may be added at any time. To ensure your bot has an up-to-date copy of the document before these keys are used, all bot instances should **refresh their local cache** of the document **at least once every 24 hours**.

The `endorsements` property within each key contains one or more endorsement strings that you can use to verify that the channel ID specified in the `channelId` property within the [Activity](bot-framework-rest-connector-api-reference#activity-object) object of the incoming request is authentic. The list of channel IDs that require endorsements is configurable within each bot. By default, it will be the list of all published channel IDs, although bot developers may override selected channel ID values either way.

### Step 4: Verify the JWT token

To verify the authenticity of the token that was sent by the Bot Connector service, you must extract the token from the `Authorization` header of the request, parse the token, verify its contents, and verify its signature.

JWT parsing libraries are available for many platforms and most implement secure and reliable parsing for JWT tokens, although you must typically configure these libraries to require that certain characteristics of the token (its issuer, audience, and so on) contain correct values. When parsing the token, you must configure the parsing library or write your own validation to ensure the token meets these requirements:

1. The token was sent in the HTTP `Authorization` header with "Bearer" scheme.
2. The token is valid JSON that conforms to the [JWT standard](http://openid.net/specs/draft-jones-json-web-token-07.html).
3. The token contains an "issuer" claim with value of `https://api.botframework.com`.
4. The token contains an "audience" claim with a value equal to the bot's Microsoft App ID.
5. The token is within its validity period. Industry-standard clock-skew is 5 minutes.
6. The token has a valid cryptographic signature, with a key listed in the OpenID keys document that was retrieved in Step 3, using the signing algorithm that is specified in the `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported` property of the Open ID Metadata document that was retrieved in Step 2.
7. The token contains a "serviceUrl" claim with value that matches the `serviceUrl` property at the root of the [Activity](bot-framework-rest-connector-api-reference#activity-object) object of the incoming request.

If endorsement for a channel ID is required:

- You should require that any `Activity` object sent to your bot with that channel ID is accompanied by a JWT token that is signed with an endorsement for that channel.
- If the endorsement isn't present, your bot should reject the request by returning an **HTTP 403 (Forbidden)** status code.

Important

All of these requirements are important, particularly requirements 4 and 6. Failure to implement ALL of these verification requirements will leave the bot open to attacks which could cause the bot to divulge its JWT token.

Implementers shouldn't expose a way to disable validation of the JWT token that is sent to the bot.

#### Connector to Bot: example JWT components

```json
header:
{
  typ: "JWT",
  alg: "RS256",
  x5t: "<SIGNING KEY ID>",
  kid: "<SIGNING KEY ID>"
},
payload:
{
  aud: "<YOU MICROSOFT APP ID>",
  iss: "https://api.botframework.com",
  nbf: 1481049243,
  exp: 1481053143,
  ... other fields follow
}
```

Note

Actual fields may vary in practice. Create and validate all JWT tokens as specified above.

## Authenticate requests from the Bot Framework Emulator to your bot

The [Bot Framework Emulator](../bot-service-debug-emulator) is a desktop tool that you can use to test the functionality of your bot. Although the Bot Framework Emulator uses the same authentication technologies as described above, it's unable to impersonate the real Bot Connector service. Instead, it uses the Microsoft App ID and Microsoft App Password that you specify when you connect the Emulator to your bot to create tokens that are identical to those that the bot creates. When the Emulator sends a request to your bot, it specifies the JWT token in the `Authorization` header of the request—in essence, using the bot's own credentials to authenticate the request.

If you're implementing an authentication library and want to accept requests from the Bot Framework Emulator, you must add this additional verification path. The path is structurally similar to the Connector -> Bot verification path, but it uses MSA's OpenID document instead of the Bot Connector's OpenID document.

To authenticate calls from the Bot Framework Emulator:

1. Your bot gets the JWT token from the authorization header in requests sent from the Bot Framework Emulator.
2. Your bot gets the OpenID metadata document for the Bot Connector service.
3. Your bot gets the list of valid signing keys from the document.
4. Your bot verifies the authenticity of the JWT token.

### Step 2: Get the MSA OpenID metadata document

The OpenID metadata document specifies the location of a second document that lists the valid signing keys. To get the MSA OpenID metadata document, issue this request via HTTPS:

```http
GET https://login.microsoftonline.com/botframework.com/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration
```

The following example shows an OpenID metadata document that is returned in response to the `GET` request. The `jwks_uri` property specifies the location of the document that contains the valid signing keys.

```json
{
    "authorization_endpoint":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/authorize",
    "token_endpoint":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/token",
    "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported":["client_secret_post","private_key_jwt"],
    "jwks_uri":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/discovery/v2.0/keys",
    ...
}
```

### Step 3: Get the list of valid signing keys

To get the list of valid signing keys, issue a `GET` request via HTTPS to the URL specified by the `jwks_uri` property in the OpenID metadata document. For example:

```http
GET https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/discovery/v2.0/keys
Host: login.microsoftonline.com
```

The response body specifies the document in the [JWK format](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7517).

### Step 4: Verify the JWT token

To verify the authenticity of the token that was sent by the Emulator, you must extract the token from the `Authorization` header of the request, parse the token, verify its contents, and verify its signature.

JWT parsing libraries are available for many platforms and most implement secure and reliable parsing for JWT tokens, although you must typically configure these libraries to require that certain characteristics of the token (its issuer, audience, and so on) contain correct values. When parsing the token, you must configure the parsing library or write your own validation to ensure the token meets these requirements:

1. The token was sent in the HTTP `Authorization` header with "Bearer" scheme.
2. The token is valid JSON that conforms to the [JWT standard](http://openid.net/specs/draft-jones-json-web-token-07.html).
3. The token contains an issuer claim for the applicable security protocol. For the current implementation, see [Microsoft.Agents.Connector](https://github.com/microsoft/Agents-for-net/tree/main/src/libraries/Client/Microsoft.Agents.Connector).
4. The token contains an "audience" claim with a value equal to the bot's Microsoft App ID.
5. The Emulator, depending on the version, sends the AppId via either the appid claim (version 1) or the authorized party claim (version 2).
6. The token is within its validity period. Industry-standard clock-skew is 5 minutes.
7. The token has a valid cryptographic signature with a key listed in the OpenID keys document that was retrieved in Step 3.

Note

Requirement 5 is a specific to the Emulator verification path.

If the token doesn't meet all of these requirements, your bot should terminate the request by returning an **HTTP 403 (Forbidden)** status code.

Important

All of these requirements are important, particularly requirements 4 and 7. Failure to implement ALL of these verification requirements will leave the bot open to attacks which could cause the bot to divulge its JWT token.

#### Emulator to Bot: example JWT components

```json
header:
{
  typ: "JWT",
  alg: "RS256",
  x5t: "<SIGNING KEY ID>",
  kid: "<SIGNING KEY ID>"
},
payload:
{
  aud: "<YOUR MICROSOFT APP ID>",
  iss: "https://sts.windows.net/d6d49420-f39b-4df7-a1dc-d59a935871db/",
  nbf: 1481049243,
  exp: 1481053143,
  ... other fields follow
}
```

Note

Actual fields may vary in practice. Create and validate all JWT tokens as specified above.

## Security protocol changes

| v3.1 & v3.2 | `https://login.microsoftonline.com/botframework.com/oauth2/v2.0/token` |

### Connector to Bot authentication

| Protocol version | Valid value |

#### OAuth login URL

| Protocol version | Valid value |

| v3.1 & v3.2 | `https://login.microsoftonline.com/botframework.com/oauth2/v2.0/token` |

#### JWT Audience

| Protocol version | Valid value |

#### JWT Issuer

| Protocol version | Valid value |
| --- | --- |
| v3.1 1.0 | `https://sts.windows.net/aaaabbbb-0000-cccc-1111-dddd2222eeee/` |

For the current implementation, see [Microsoft.Agents.Connector](https://github.com/microsoft/Agents-for-net/tree/main/src/libraries/Client/Microsoft.Agents.Connector).

content.content:
**Worker size (free and paid):** Both plans have a 64 MiB limit on uncompressed size. The page says, "There is no compressed size limit. Only the uncompressed bundle size counts." Compressed size isn't capped.

**Startup time:** The limit is 1 second. The page states, "A Worker must parse and execute its global scope (top-level code outside of handlers) within 1 second."

**Cold start and bundle size:** The page doesn't use the term "cold start." It does say, "Larger Worker bundles can impact startup time," which is the closest statement to your question. It also notes that expensive initialization in global scope increases startup time.

**Memory per isolate:** The limit is 128 MB. The page says, "Each isolate can consume up to 128 MB of memory," including JavaScript heap and WebAssembly allocations.

# Get user - Microsoft Graph v1.0 | Microsoft Learn

Namespace: microsoft.graph

Retrieve the properties and relationships of [user](resources/user) object.

This operation returns by default only a subset of the more commonly used properties for each user. These *default* properties are noted in the [Properties](resources/user#properties) section. To get properties that are *not* returned by default, do a [GET operation](user-get) for the user and specify the properties in a `$select` OData query option. Because the **user** resource supports [extensions](/en-us/graph/extensibility-overview), you can also use the `GET` operation to get custom properties and extension data in a **user** instance.

Customers through Microsoft Entra ID for customers can also use this API operation to retrieve their details.

This API is available in the following [national cloud deployments](/en-us/graph/deployments).

| Global service | US Government L4 | US Government L5 (DOD) | China operated by 21Vianet |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Permissions

Choose the permission or permissions marked as least privileged for this API. Use a higher privileged permission or permissions [only if your app requires it](/en-us/graph/permissions-overview#best-practices-for-using-microsoft-graph-permissions). For details about delegated and application permissions, see [Permission types](/en-us/graph/permissions-overview#permission-types). To learn more about these permissions, see the [permissions reference](/en-us/graph/permissions-reference).

| Permission type | Least privileged permissions | Higher privileged permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delegated (work or school account) | User.Read | User.ReadWrite, User.ReadBasic.All, User.Read.All, User.ReadWrite.All, Directory.Read.All, Directory.ReadWrite.All |
| Delegated (personal Microsoft account) | User.Read | User.ReadWrite |
| Application | User.Read.All | User.ReadWrite.All, Directory.Read.All, Directory.ReadWrite.All |

Note

The `User.Read` permission allows the app to read the profile, and discover relationships such as the group membership, reports, and manager of the signed-in user only.

### Permissions for specific scenarios

- To read the **employeeLeaveDateTime**property:
    - In delegated scenarios, the signed-in user needs at least one of the following Microsoft Entra roles: *Lifecycle Workflows Administrator* (least privilege), *Global Reader*; the app must be granted the *User-LifeCycleInfo.Read.All* delegated permission.
    - In app-only scenarios with Microsoft Graph permissions, the app must be granted the *User-LifeCycleInfo.Read.All* permission.
- To read the **customSecurityAttributes**property:
    - In delegated scenarios, the signed-in user must be assigned the *Attribute Assignment Administrator* role and the app granted the *CustomSecAttributeAssignment.Read.All* permission.
    - In app-only scenarios with Microsoft Graph permissions, the app must be granted the *CustomSecAttributeAssignment.Read.All* permission.
- *User-Mail.ReadWrite.All* is the least privileged permission to read and write the **otherMails** property; also allows to read some identifier-related properties on the user object.
- *User-PasswordProfile.ReadWrite.All* is the least privileged permission to read and write password reset-related properties; also allows to read some identifier-related properties on the user object.
- *User-Phone.ReadWrite.All* is the least privileged permission to read and write the **businessPhones** and **mobilePhone** properties; also allows to read some identifier-related properties on the user object.
- *User.EnableDisableAccount.All* + *User.Read.All* is the least privileged combination of permissions to read and write the **accountEnabled** property.

## HTTP request

For a specific user:

```http
GET /me
GET /users/{id | userPrincipalName}
```

Note

Calling the `/me` endpoint requires a signed-in user and therefore a delegated permission. Application permissions aren't supported when using the `/me` endpoint.

Tip

- When the **userPrincipalName** begins with a `$` character, the GET request URL syntax `/users/$x@y.com` fails with a `400 Bad Request` error code. The request fails because the URL violates the OData URL convention, which expects only system query options to be prefixed with a `$` character. Remove the slash (/) after `/users` and enclose the **userPrincipalName** in parentheses and single quotes, as follows: `/users('$x@y.com')`. For example, `/users('$AdeleVance@contoso.com')`.
- To query a B2B user using the **userPrincipalName**, encode the hash (#) character. That is, replace the `#` symbol with `%23`. For example, `/users/AdeleVance_adatum.com%23EXT%23@contoso.com`.

For the signed-in user:

```http
GET /me
```

Note

Calling the `/me` endpoint requires a signed-in user and therefore a delegated permission. Application permissions aren't supported when using the `/me` endpoint.

## Optional query parameters

This method supports the `$select`[OData query parameter](/en-us/graph/query-parameters) to retrieve specific user properties, including those not returned by default.

By default, only a limited set of properties are returned (*businessPhones, displayName, givenName, id, jobTitle, mail, mobilePhone, officeLocation, preferredLanguage, surname, userPrincipalName*).

To return an alternative property set, you must specify the desired set of [user](resources/user) properties using the OData `$select` query parameter. For example, to return *displayName*, *givenName*, and *postalCode*, add the following expression to your query `$select=displayName,givenName,postalCode`.

Extension properties also support query parameters as follows:

| Extension type | Comments |
| --- | --- |
| onPremisesExtensionAttributes 1-15 | Returned only with `$select`. |
| Schema extensions | Returned only with `$select`. |
| Open extensions | Returned only through the [Get open extension](opentypeextension-get) operation. |
| Directory extensions | Returned only with `$select`. |

## Request headers

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Authorization | Bearer {token}. Required. Learn more about [authentication and authorization](/en-us/graph/auth/auth-concepts). |

## Request body

Don't supply a request body for this method.

## Response

If successful, this method returns a `200 OK` response code and [user](resources/user) object in the response body. It returns the default properties unless you use `$select` to specify specific properties. This method returns `202 Accepted` when the request has been processed successfully but the server requires more time to complete related background operations.

If a user with the ID doesn't exist, this method returns a `404 Not Found` error code.

### Example 3: Use $select to retrieve specific properties of a user

To retrieve specific properties, use the OData `$select` query parameter. For example, to return *displayName*, *givenName*, *postalCode*, and *identities*, add the following query expression to your query `$select=displayName,givenName,postalCode,identities`

#### Request

# [HTTP](#tab/http)
```msgraph
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/87d349ed-44d7-43e1-9a83-5f2406dee5bd?$select=displayName,givenName,postalCode,identities
```

{requestConfiguration.QueryParameters.Select = new string []{ "displayName","givenName","postalCode","identities" };

- **`team.id`:** The example includes `team.id`. The field list describes `team` as "The workspace the app is installed on. Null if the app is org-installed."

- **`response_url`:** Listed as optional and deprecated for apps built with the Deno Slack SDK. The field list describes it as "A short-lived webhook that can be used to send messages in response to interactions."

# Overview - Publish your agent or app - Teams | Microsoft Learn

There are two ways to distribute your Microsoft Teams agent or app:

- **Publish to your organization**: Make your agent or app available to people within your organization. Requires your Teams admin's approval.
- **Publish your agent or app to the Teams Store**: Make your agent or app available to everyone on the Teams Store. Requires Microsoft approval.

How you publish depends on several factors including users' needs, business, technical requirements, and your goals for the agent or app.

## Publish to your organization

Teams agent or apps can be distributed privately within an organization and do not need to be published to the Teams Store for tenant-internal use. Availability to users can be controlled through Teams admin policies and app setup controls in the customer tenant. For more information, see [manage your apps in the Teams admin center](/en-us/microsoftteams/manage-apps?toc=%2Fmicrosoftteams%2Fplatform%2Ftoc.json&bc=%2FMicrosoftTeams%2Fbreadcrumb%2Ftoc.json).

### Government Community Cloud (GCC) organizations

In GCC Teams environments, compliant Microsoft agent or apps are enabled by default. Before publishing an agent or app, however, make sure that all the agent or app's endpoints comply with your GCC organization's requirements. For more information, see [Government Community Cloud](../cloud-overview#teams-app-capabilities).

Important

If your agent or app includes a bot or message extension, you must select the **Microsoft Teams for Government** option when setting up a channel between your bot and Teams in Azure. For more information, see [connect a bot to channels](/en-us/azure/bot-service/bot-service-manage-channels?view=azure-bot-service-4.0&preserve-view=true).

## Publish your agent or app to the Teams Store

You can publish your agent or app directly to the Microsoft Teams Store inside Microsoft Teams and reach millions of users around the world. If your app is also featured in the Teams Store, you can instantly reach potential customers. For more information, see [publish to the Teams Store](appsource/publish).

### Enable customization for your Microsoft Teams agent or app

You can allow customers to customize some aspects of your Microsoft Teams agent or app in the Teams admin center. This feature is supported only for apps published to the Microsoft Teams Store. For more information, see [Enable customization for your Microsoft Teams app](../design/enable-app-customization)

## Before you publish

Before you publish your agent or app, complete the following steps to ensure your agent or app is ready for distribution.

### Configure default install options

You can configure default install options. For example, if your agent or app's primary capability is a bot, you can make the bot the default capability when a user installs your agent or app to a team. For more information, see [Configure default options for Teams app](add-default-install-scope)

### Create Teams agent or app package

To publish your Teams agent or app, you must have a valid app package. An app package is a zip file that contains an **app manifest** and **app icons**. For more information, see [Teams app package](../build-and-test/apps-package)

### Upload your agent or app in Teams

Upload a custom agent or app for personal use, collaborating with your team, or testing and debugging. This kind of distribution doesn't require a formal review process.

Important

Uploading custom agent or apps are available in Government Community Cloud (GCC) but aren't available in GCC High, Department of Defense (DoD), and Teams operated by 21Vianet.

For more information, see [upload your app in Teams](apps-upload).

# Can `vercel/chat` run on Cloudflare Workers with Alchemy and Effect 4 for Slack and Microsoft Teams?

Research for issue #297 (map #295, blocks #298). This is throwaway research and will not be merged.
Context: SPEC.md §5.1 and §5.7 (Slack and Teams Channels), §6 (Cloudflare only: Workers, Durable Objects, D1; no external store or relay), ADR 0005 (the Invitation token travels in the URL fragment and reaches only the Submission Worker), ADR 0007 (a rating link only preselects), ADR 0008 (Effect and Alchemy stay in `packages/cloudflare`; answer entry has a tight budget). Pins checked in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` on `origin/main` at `32216f8c`: `effect` 4.1.4, `alchemy` 2.0.0-beta.87.

Researched 2026-11-20 against `chat`, `@chat-adapter/slack`, `@chat-adapter/teams` and `@chat-adapter/state-memory` **4.45.0** (published 2026-11-13), read from the npm tarballs. "Spike" below means a throwaway Worker I bundled with esbuild 0.28.2 and ran in local workerd 1.20261026.1 (`compatibilityDate = "2026-10-01"`, `nodejs_compat`). The spike code is not committed. Claims marked *(secondary)* come from a forum or Q&A thread, not vendor docs or source.

## TL;DR

1. **It runs, but heavily.** Both adapters load and work in workerd: Slack signature checks, a slash command handler, and outbound Slack Web API calls work, and so do Teams JWT checks against Microsoft's live JWKS and an MSAL token request to Entra ID. The cost is size. Core alone is 266 KB minified (79 KB gzip), with Slack 692 KB (188 KB), with Teams 2.39 MB (617 KB), and with both 2.79 MB (745 KB). Teams pulls in `express`, `@azure/msal-node`, `jsonwebtoken`, `jwks-rsa`, `axios`, `@microsoft/signalr` and a 372 KB Graph endpoint table.
2. **It needs a state store, and the only fits are a Durable Object or an in-memory adapter.** `Chat` requires a `StateAdapter` ("**required**"). The official production adapters are Redis, ioredis and PostgreSQL, so none of them fits SPEC §6. A community `chat-state-cloudflare-do` (v0.2.0, one maintainer) exists, or we could write our own on the Organization DO. Multi-workspace Slack keeps bot tokens in that store, and both adapters cache personal data in it: Slack caches name, email and avatar for 8 days, Teams caches tenant, AAD object ID and service URL for 30 days.
3. **Its link button breaks ADR 0005 on Slack.** `LinkButton` renders as a Block Kit button with `url`, and Slack sends an interaction payload for every click. The default `action_id` is `link-${url.slice(0,200)}`, so the Invitation token (in the fragment) would arrive at MainWorker together with the clicking Person's Slack user ID. `CardLink` (a plain `<url|label>`) avoids this. We would then use the SDK only to post text, which a thin adapter does with one `fetch`.
4. **Our surface is small and outbound-first.** We need to post, edit and delete messages, take one slash command, verify two webhook signatures and run two install flows. A thin Effect adapter per platform is about 5–15 KB and decodes with Effect Schema. It keeps state in the Organization DO beside the Person and logs only what we choose. **Recommendation: thin Effect adapters, not `vercel/chat`.** Details and ADR constraints are at the end.
5. **Open, needs a live test:** whether Teams (Safe Links click-time check, desktop, mobile, web) keeps the `#t=…&v=…` fragment; whether a plain Slack mrkdwn link sends any event when clicked; whether a single-tenant Azure Bot can proactively message users in customer tenants.

## 1. Workerd compatibility and bundle footprint

### What the packages import

Read from `dist/*.js` in each tarball:

- `chat`: `async_hooks`, `crypto`, `unified`/`remark-*` (Markdown AST), `@workflow/serde`. `ai`, `zod` and `workflow` are optional peers (`npm view chat peerDependenciesMeta`).
- `@chat-adapter/slack`: `@slack/web-api` (axios, p-queue, form-data), and a **static** `import { SocketModeClient } from "@slack/socket-mode"` (pulls in `ws`), even though we only need webhook mode. It also imports `async_hooks` and `crypto`.
- `@chat-adapter/shared`: `dns/promises`, `https`, `net` (`BlockList`), `stream`, `zlib`, for the guarded file-download transport.
- `@chat-adapter/teams`: `@microsoft/teams.apps` 2.2.1, which depends on `express` 5, `cors`, `@azure/msal-node`, `jsonwebtoken`, `jwks-rsa`, `axios`, `@microsoft/signalr`, `@opentelemetry/api` and `reflect-metadata`. It also depends on `teams.api`, `teams.cards`, `teams.graph` and `teams.graph-endpoints` (from `npm view` of each package).

### Spike results

Measured with esbuild bundling for workerd (`--platform=node --conditions=workerd,worker,browser --minify`, Node built-ins external):

| Entry | Minified | gzip -9 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `chat` + memory state, no adapter | 272,280 B | 80,544 B |
| + Slack adapter | 708,852 B | 192,782 B |
| + Teams adapter | 2,444,832 B | 632,256 B |
| + Slack and Teams | 2,786,720 B | 744,724 B |

The largest contributors to the combined bundle (esbuild metafile, bytes in output): `iconv-lite` 482 KB, `@microsoft/teams.graph-endpoints` 372 KB, `mime-db` 280 KB, `@azure/msal-node` 188 KB, `@microsoft/teams.apps` 162 KB, `axios` 144 KB, `@chat-adapter/slack` 103 KB, `chat` 95 KB.

Behaviour in workerd 1.20261026.1 with `nodejs_compat`:

- **Module load.** The first build failed at startup with `Dynamic require of "node:os" is not supported`, because the CommonJS dependencies `require()` Node built-ins inside an ESM bundle. A `createRequire` banner fixed it. Alchemy's bundler uses an unenv-based `nodejs-compat` rolldown plugin (`@alchemy.run/cloudflare-runtime/dist/rolldown/plugins/nodejs-compat.js`) that is meant to handle this. I did not build the spike through Alchemy, so **a real Alchemy build is still unverified**.
- **Slack inbound.** A bad signature returned `401 Invalid signature`. A timestamp 10 minutes old was rejected ("Slack timestamp is too old"). A correctly signed `/pulse` slash command returned `200` and ran the handler through `waitUntil`.
- **Slack outbound.** The first webhook triggered `auth.test` (adapter initialization), and the slash command handler called `users.info` for the invoking user. Both requests went through axios to a mock API. If the API is unreachable, `@slack/web-api` retries for minutes inside the request, which is a cold-start latency risk against Slack's 3-second acknowledgement window ([Slack: handling user interaction](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction)).
- **Teams inbound.** A missing `Authorization` header returned `401 Missing authorization header`. A forged JWT returned `401 JWT validation failed`, after `jwks-rsa` fetched Microsoft's live signing keys from workerd.
- **Teams outbound.** `openDM` ran MSAL's client-credentials flow from workerd and got a real Entra ID error back (`AADSTS700038 … is not a valid application identifier`). The token path works. Sending a message needs a real bot.
- **Logging.** `new Chat({ logger: "silent" })` did not silence the adapters. `[chat-sdk:slack] …` and `[ERROR] @teams/app/jwt-validator …` lines still reached the console, and the adapters' own default is `ConsoleLogger("info")` (Slack and Teams READMEs, `logger` option). MainWorker has Workers Logs on, so each adapter needs its own logger, and the Teams SDK's internal logger needs separate wiring.

Cloudflare limits are 64 MiB uncompressed, with no compressed limit. Startup has a 1-second limit to "parse and execute its global scope", and "Larger Worker bundles can impact startup time" ([Workers limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/)). Adding 2.8 MB fits the size limit, but it would make MainWorker's cold start larger. Our local timing was too noisy to report. An Alchemy deploy of a preview stage would give the real startup figure.

**Effect 4 fit.** The SDK is a Promise and class API with a mutable singleton (`new Chat`, `bot.onSlashCommand`, `bot.webhooks.slack(request, { waitUntil })`). It uses `AsyncLocalStorage` for per-call bot tokens (`withBotToken`, Slack README). It works behind `Effect.tryPromise`, but errors, retries and timeouts stay inside axios and p-retry instead of being typed, which goes against SPEC §6.1 ("Errors, dependencies, retries, and timeouts are typed").

## 2. Webhook signature verification and stateless handling in MainWorker

**Slack.** The signature is `v0=` plus the HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of `v0:{X-Slack-Request-Timestamp}:{raw body}`, keyed by the signing secret. Verify it over the raw body before parsing, with a constant-time compare. The documented example rejects timestamps more than 5 minutes off as a possible replay ([Verifying requests from Slack](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/verifying-requests-from-slack)). The adapter does this (spike above). If you pass a custom `webhookVerifier`, "you are responsible for replay/timestamp protection" (Slack README). In Workers, the whole check is `crypto.subtle.importKey` + `sign` + compare, about 30 lines. Interactions and slash commands must be acknowledged within 3 seconds ([handling user interaction](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction)). Ack first, then run the work in `ctx.waitUntil` or a Queue.

**Teams (Bot Connector).** The bot must verify the inbound `Authorization: Bearer` JWT. The issuer must be `https://api.botframework.com`, the audience must be the bot's App ID, the token must be in date (5 min skew), the signature must use a key from `https://login.botframework.com/v1/.well-known/openidconfiguration` → `jwks_uri` (refresh at least every 24 h), and the `serviceUrl` claim must match the activity's `serviceUrl`. Channel endorsements are checked where required ([Bot Connector authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bot-service/rest-api/bot-framework-rest-connector-authentication)). That is RS256 via `crypto.subtle.verify` plus a JWKS cache (a `caches.default` entry or a module-scope value with a TTL). Outbound calls use a client-credentials token from `login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token` with scope `https://api.botframework.com/.default`, valid for 3600 s, which we should cache (same page).

**Stateless?** Signature checks need no state. The SDK still touches state on every webhook. It deduplicates Slack retries by `event_id` through the state adapter, takes a per-thread lock for message events, and caches user profiles (Slack README "Enterprise Grid"; `chat/docs/state-adapters.mdx`). With the memory adapter those are per-isolate and lost on eviction. For a slash-command-only inbound surface we don't need any of it: Slack slash commands are not retried as events, and the reply goes to `response_url` or an ephemeral message.

## 3. Is a Durable Object SQLite `StateAdapter` needed?

**Short answer:** with `vercel/chat`, yes, or we accept per-isolate memory state. With thin adapters, no separate adapter is needed. The few records we keep are ordinary rows in the Organization DO and D1.

- `ChatConfig.state` is **required** ("State adapter for subscriptions, locking, and dedup", `chat/README.md`). The `StateAdapter` interface has 19 methods: locks, `setIfNotExists`, lists, queues, subscriptions and key/value with TTL (`chat/dist/types-*.d.ts`).
- Official production adapters: Redis, ioredis, PostgreSQL. The docs point Vercel users to Upstash, Redis Cloud, Neon or Supabase ([state adapters doc](https://chat-sdk.dev/docs/state-adapters), mirrored at `chat/docs/state-adapters.mdx`). **All are third-party stores and break SPEC §6.** "In production, use Redis, ioredis, or PostgreSQL."
- **What lands in state:**
  - Slack multi-workspace mode stores each installation (bot token, optionally AES-GCM encrypted with `SLACK_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) under `slack:installation:{teamId}`. An `installationProvider` can make token reads come from our own store, but `handleOAuthCallback`, `setInstallation` and `deleteInstallation` still write to the state adapter (Slack README).
  - Slack `getUser` caches `{displayName, realName, email, avatarUrl}` for 8 days, plus a name→ID reverse index (`USER_CACHE_TTL_MS`, `@chat-adapter/slack/dist/index.js` ~L2380).
  - Teams caches `teams:serviceUrl:`, `teams:tenantId:` and `teams:aadObjectId:` per user for 30 days (`CACHE_TTL_MS`, `@chat-adapter/teams/dist/index.js` L2082, L2351). `openDM` throws "User must interact with the bot first … to cache their tenant ID" when the tenant isn't cached (L3480).
- An existing Cloudflare option is `chat-state-cloudflare-do` 0.2.0 (MIT, 54 stars, last push 2026-07-02). It is a SQLite-backed DO with its own class and binding ([repo](https://github.com/dcartertwo/chat-state-cloudflare-do)). It would be a second DO namespace outside the Organization DO, holding personal data and bot tokens that GDPR export and erasure (#306, #307) would have to cover separately.
- Our surface (outbound Invitations, Reminders and Shared Results; one slash command; install callbacks) needs **none** of subscriptions, thread locks, message queues or history. What it does need is durable and belongs to the Organization (§5 below).

## 4. Card rendering fidelity

**What we post** (SPEC §5.1, #298 decisions on #295): an Invitation with a title, the anonymity line, five 1-tap rating links and "Open check-in"; a Reminder; a Shared Results summary (no comments, counts or Discussion guide). Unfurls must be off. Messages are edited later to remove answer links.

**Slack (Block Kit).**
- A `section` with mrkdwn text and `<url|label>` links renders all of this. A plain link is not an interactive component. The documented interaction payloads are `block_actions`, `shortcut`/`message_actions`, `view_submission` and `view_closed` ([handling user interaction](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction)). None of them is a hyperlink in text. The docs don't say outright that a plain link sends nothing, so this needs a live test (§7).
- **URL buttons do send a payload.** The button element docs say: "If you're using url, you'll still receive an interaction payload and will need to send an acknowledgement response" ([button element](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/block-elements/button-element)). The `block_actions` payload carries `user.id`, `team.id`, `action_id` and the `message` the block is in ([block_actions payload](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/interaction-payloads/block_actions-payload)), and that message contains the button URL with our fragment token. **So the Invitation must use text links, not buttons**, or the token and the Person's identity reach MainWorker on every tap.
- Unfurling: "By default, we unfurl all links in messages posted by users and Slack apps", and "Slack crawls the URL". Set `unfurl_links: false` and `unfurl_media: false` ([unfurling links](https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/unfurling-links-in-messages)). A crawler GET never carries the fragment, so even a missed unfurl leaks no token (ADR 0005). The Chat SDK adapter already sets both flags to `false` on every `chat.postMessage` (`index.js` L4623, L4651).
- `vercel/chat` mapping: `CardLink` → `<url|label>` (fine). `LinkButton` → `{type:"button", url, action_id: button.id ?? \`link-${button.url.slice(0,200)}\`}` (`@chat-adapter/slack/dist/index.js` L288–300), which puts the token in `action_id` as well. `Table` → Slack data table. No other element covers something we can't write by hand.

**Teams (Adaptive Cards).**
- `TextBlock`s plus an `ActionSet` of `Action.OpenUrl` render the Invitation. `Action.OpenUrl` "opens a specified URL in the user's browser". Only `Action.Execute`/`Action.Submit` send an `adaptiveCard/action` invoke to the bot ([card actions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/task-modules-and-cards/cards/cards-actions)). Unlike Slack, a Teams link button does not call us. The target domain must be in the manifest's `validDomains`, or Teams shows "URL may lead to untrusted content" (same page). The Microsoft examples use card `version: "1.5"`.
- `vercel/chat` maps `LinkButton` → `Action.OpenUrl` (`@chat-adapter/teams/dist/cards.js` L233). But if a card contains any input, it appends an automatic `__auto_submit` action (L214), which is an `Action.Submit` path we would not want.
- Editing the message later uses `PUT {serviceUrl}/v3/conversations/{conversationId}/activities/{activityId}`, so we must keep the activity ID returned by the post ([proactive messages](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/conversations/send-proactive-messages)).

**Verdict on fidelity.** The SDK's lowest-common-denominator JSX produces acceptable Block Kit and Adaptive Cards, but its interactive defaults work against us (Slack link buttons, Teams auto-submit). Our three message types are short, fixed templates. Hand-written JSON built from Effect Schema types, with strings from the messages catalog, gives full control and can be snapshot-tested.

## 5. Teams proactive messages: what an unprompted Invitation needs

From [Send proactive messages](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/conversations/send-proactive-messages) (updated 2026-11-15) and [Proactively install your bot with Graph](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/graph-api/proactive-bots-and-messages/graph-proactive-bots-and-messages) (updated 2026-08-03):

- **The app must be installed for the user.** "For a user to receive proactive messages, install the app for the user or make the user a part of a team in which the app is installed." Sending by `aadObjectId` without a personal install returns `403 ForbiddenOperationException`.
- **Email cannot address a user:** "Email addresses and User Principal Names (UPNs) can't be used to address proactive messages in any scope." We need the Person's Entra object ID: from the install or `conversationUpdate` activity, or from Graph `GET /users/{upn}`, which needs the application permission `User.Read.All` ([Get user](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/user-get?view=graph-rest-1.0)).
- **Proactive install** needs the application permission `TeamsAppInstallation.ReadWriteSelfForUser.All`, a `webApplicationInfo` entry in the manifest, and **explicit admin consent in the customer's tenant**. "Microsoft Graph can only install apps published to your organization's app store or the Microsoft Teams Store."
- **Create the conversation once and store it.** You need `aadObjectId` or `userId`, `tenantId` and `serviceUrl`, then call `POST {serviceUrl}/v3/conversations`. "Create the conversation only once, and store the resulting `conversationId` for future proactive messages." Use the `serviceUrl` from an incoming activity. `https://smba.trafficmanager.net/teams/` is the public fallback. A blocked or uninstalled bot gets `403` with `subCode: MessageWritesBlocked`, which we can map to "fall back to Email".
- **Azure Bot registration.** "Multi-tenant bot creation will be deprecated after July 31, 2025." New bots are single-tenant or user-assigned managed identity ([Create an Azure Bot resource](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bot-service/abs-quickstart)). Managed identity needs an Azure-hosted token endpoint, which a Worker can't use, so **a single-tenant bot with a client secret (or certificate)** is the realistic choice. Microsoft documents no official path for a single-tenant bot reaching users in other tenants. Q&A threads say Teams Store publication makes it work, and others report cross-tenant auth failures *(secondary)* ([Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5645637/how-to-enable-a-multi-tenant-one-on-one-bot-in-mic), [Tech Community](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/teamsdeveloper/questions-about-alternatives-to-multi-tenant-bots-after-july-31-2025-deprecation/4423676)). Neither SDK changes this.
- **Where the reference lives.**
  - Per Person: `{tenantId, aadObjectId, conversationId, serviceUrl}`. It is personal data that belongs to one Person in one Organization and must go with GDPR export and erasure (#306, #307). It belongs in the **Organization DO**, next to the Person's preferred Channel.
  - The posted `activityId` per Invitation (for the later edit) is also stored there.
  - D1 holds only the lookup that must happen before the Organization is known: `teams tenantId → OrganizationId` and `slack team_id/enterprise_id → OrganizationId`, as SPEC §6.2 already lists ("Slack and Teams workspace to organization").

## 6. App registration and OAuth installation per Organization

**Slack.**
- One SurveyBeat Slack app. Each Organization installs it into its workspace through OAuth v2. Redirect to `slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize` with a `state`, the `code` expires after 10 minutes, then call `oauth.v2.access` and get a bot token plus `team.id` (or `enterprise.id` with `is_enterprise_install`). "OAuth tokens do not expire" unless token rotation is turned on ([Installing with OAuth](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/installing-with-oauth)).
- Installing outside the owning workspace needs public distribution (`invalid_team_for_non_distributed_app` otherwise).
- Scopes for our surface: `chat:write`, `im:write` (open DMs), `commands`, and `users:read.email` for `users.lookupByEmail` (Tier 3) to map a Person's email to a Slack user ([users.lookupByEmail](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/users.lookupByEmail)).
- Marketplace: since 2025-05-29, unlisted commercially distributed apps get 1 request/min on `conversations.history`/`replies`. Slack says "the Slack Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercially distributing apps" ([changelog](https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/05/29/rate-limit-changes-for-non-marketplace-apps)). We don't call those methods, but Marketplace review is a business and legal step before customers outside our own workspace.

**Microsoft Teams.**
- One Entra app registration plus one Azure Bot resource (single-tenant, see §5), and one Teams app package (manifest with `bots`, `validDomains`, `webApplicationInfo`).
- Each customer gets it through their org catalog (the Teams admin approves an upload) or the Teams Store (Microsoft validation) ([Publish overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/concepts/deploy-and-publish/apps-publish-overview)). Their Entra admin then grants consent for `TeamsAppInstallation.ReadWriteSelfForUser.All` and `User.Read.All`.
- There is no per-install bot token as in Slack. The bot's own credential works in every tenant, and the per-Organization state is the tenant ID and conversation references.
- Infra: the Azure resources live outside Alchemy's Cloudflare provider. They are created once by hand or with the Teams CLI (`teams app create`, Teams README) and recorded in `docs/infra.md`. Only the App ID, secret and tenant ID enter Alchemy as Worker secrets.

## 7. The two link questions

### Microsoft Teams Safe Links and the `#t=…&v=…` fragment — not settled

What the docs say ([Safe Links overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-links-about), updated 2026-10-29):

- "URLs in Teams are checked against a list of known malicious links when the protected user clicks the link (time-of-click protection). **URLs aren't rewritten.**"
- "the intermediary page that does Safe Links validation redirects to the target page, which is treated as a cross-site request". So a Safe Links page sits between the click and our page.
- Built-in protection applies Safe Links in Teams to every user in a tenant with at least one Defender for Office 365 license, and the "Do not rewrite" list is not honoured by Teams.

What that implies, and why it is not settled:

- An HTTP 3xx keeps the original fragment when `Location` has none (RFC 9110 §10.2.2), and a time-of-click lookup on the server never sees the fragment.
- If the intermediary passes our URL as a query parameter, or navigates with script, whether `#t=…&v=…` survives depends on Microsoft's implementation, which is not documented.
- Teams desktop, web and mobile also open links through different shells.
- I found no primary source either way.

Test that settles it: in an M365 tenant with a Defender for Office 365 P1 trial, Safe Links for Teams on, and a sideloaded test bot, post an Adaptive Card with `Action.OpenUrl` and a plain Markdown link to `https://<preview>/a#t=TEST&v=3`. Click each on Teams desktop (Windows and macOS), web and iOS/Android. Use a test `answer.html` that renders `location.hash`. If any client drops it, Teams Invitations offer only "Open check-in" (the Teams fallback named in #295). Even if the fragment is lost, the token never reaches a server, because a dropped fragment is simply gone.

### Slack plain links send no event — documented by omission, test to confirm

- The documented interaction payload types (§4) are all triggered by interactive components, shortcuts or modals. `link_shared` fires only for an app's registered App Unfurl Domains (needs `links:read`), and "is not dispatched for messages posted by an app" ([unfurling links](https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/unfurling-links-in-messages)). So a plain `<url|label>` in a message the app posted, with no unfurl domain registered, has no documented path to our request URL. A URL **button** does send a `block_actions` payload (§4).
- Test that settles it: in a test workspace, have the app post a message with a mrkdwn link and a URL button, Interactivity and Event Subscriptions on, and the request URL pointing at a logging endpoint. Click both on desktop, web and mobile, and confirm that only the button produces a request.

## 8. Recommendation

**Build thin Effect adapters for Slack and Microsoft Teams behind the `ChannelSender` port. Do not adopt `vercel/chat`.**

Why:

- **Fit to the surface.** We need post, edit and delete for three fixed templates, one slash command, two signature checks and two install flows. `vercel/chat` is built for conversational bots (subscriptions, thread locks, streaming, AI SDK, history), and those features are why it requires a state store.
- **Cloudflare-only.** Its only official production stores are Redis and Postgres. Using it means writing or adopting a DO `StateAdapter` (19 methods) that holds bot tokens and cached personal data outside the Organization DO.
- **Privacy defaults.** The Slack `LinkButton` routes the Invitation token and the clicker's identity to MainWorker. The adapters cache emails and names for 8–30 days. Adapter loggers ignore `logger: "silent"`. Each needs a workaround, and each workaround is a place for a regression in a release-blocking invariant (SPEC §7).
- **Footprint and toolchain.** It adds 2.8 MB minified to MainWorker, with Express, MSAL and axios inside a Worker, Promise-typed errors, and retries we don't control. The thin adapters use `fetch`, `crypto.subtle` and Effect Schema, the same pattern as `CloudflareEmailSender`.
- **What we give up.** Ready-made OAuth callback handling, Slack Enterprise Grid quirks (shared channels, `enterprise_id` keys), and a cross-platform card DSL. The first two are worth copying from the adapter source as a reference. The third we don't need.

Revisit `vercel/chat` only if a later release adds two-way conversational features (for example "Ask your results" in chat, R5). Even then, put it in a separate Worker, so that MainWorker and the answer path stay small.

## 9. Constraints for the Channel delivery ADR

1. **No answers through chat.** Chat messages carry only links to `answer.html` (`/a#t=<token>&v=<n>`). No Slack Block Kit `button` (URL buttons send `block_actions`), no Teams `Action.Submit`/`Action.Execute`, no modals for answering. Inbound interaction endpoints accept only the slash command and install and uninstall events. Any other payload type gets `200` with no processing and no logging of its body.
2. **The Invitation token stays in the fragment** (ADR 0005), and the Channel adapter never logs a message body, URL or recipient ID. Adapters run in MainWorker or a Queue consumer, never in SubmissionWorker.
3. **Unfurls off.** Slack posts set `unfurl_links:false, unfurl_media:false`. Our domain is registered as no App Unfurl Domain. Teams uses Adaptive Cards (no link preview).
4. **Signature checks before parsing.**
   - Slack: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, constant-time compare, reject a timestamp older than 300 s.
   - Teams: RS256 JWT, `iss=https://api.botframework.com`, `aud=<AppId>`, 5-minute skew, `serviceUrl` claim equal to the activity's, JWKS from the Bot Framework OpenID document refreshed at least every 24 h.
   - Both run with `crypto.subtle`, with no Node crypto, Express or MSAL.
5. **Acknowledge within 3 s.** Slack slash commands answer at once and do the work in `waitUntil` or a Queue. Outbound sends go through the existing Queue with retries and a DLQ (SPEC §6.2), and every step is idempotent per (Invitation, Channel).
6. **Storage split.**
   - **D1:** only `slack team_id|enterprise_id → OrganizationId` and `teams tenantId → OrganizationId`.
   - **Organization DO:** the Slack installation (bot token encrypted with a Worker secret), each Person's Channel identity (Slack user ID, or Teams `aadObjectId` + `conversationId` + `serviceUrl`), and per-Invitation message handles (Slack `channel`+`ts`, Teams `activityId`) for the later edit.
   - No separate chat state store. GDPR export and erasure (#306, #307) cover these rows.
7. **No cached profiles.** Store only the IDs needed to deliver. Never store Slack or Teams display names, emails or avatars. Map email → platform ID once, when a Person picks the Channel (`users.lookupByEmail`, or Graph `GET /users/{upn}`), and keep only the ID.
8. **Edit-after-answer has no timing signal.** Remove answer links at Round close or in a periodic batch, not on each Submission. Otherwise the platform records a per-Person edit time that sits next to "answered" (ADR 0005 stores no time for Participation).
9. **App-level secrets via Alchemy** (Slack signing secret, client ID and secret; Teams App ID, secret, tenant ID; token-encryption key). The Azure Bot, Entra app and Teams package are set up outside Alchemy, by hand or with the Teams CLI, and documented in `docs/infra.md`.
10. **Teams prerequisites are explicit in the product.** The customer's Teams admin must make the app available (org catalog or Store), and their Entra admin must consent to `TeamsAppInstallation.ReadWriteSelfForUser.All` and `User.Read.All`. Until both are true for a Person, that Person's Invitations go by Email. A `403 MessageWritesBlocked` falls back to Email.
11. **Teams one-tap depends on the Safe Links test (§7).** If any supported Teams client drops the fragment, Teams Invitations carry only "Open check-in".
12. **Slack ships first** (map #295). Before external customers, decide on Marketplace listing, and on whether Slack and Microsoft are sub-processors (#305).
13. **Size budget.** The Slack and Teams adapters together add at most ~50 KB minified to MainWorker. A dependency that pulls in `express`, `axios`, `@azure/msal-node` or `ws` needs an ADR.

## Sources

Package source (npm tarballs, version 4.45.0): `chat/README.md`, `chat/docs/state-adapters.mdx`, `chat/docs/cards.mdx`, `chat/dist/types-*.d.ts`, `@chat-adapter/slack/README.md` and `dist/index.js`, `@chat-adapter/teams/README.md`, `dist/index.js` and `dist/cards.js`, `@chat-adapter/shared/dist/index.js`. Repository: [vercel/chat](https://github.com/vercel/chat). Community DO adapter: [dcartertwo/chat-state-cloudflare-do](https://github.com/dcartertwo/chat-state-cloudflare-do).

Slack: [verifying requests](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/verifying-requests-from-slack), [handling user interaction](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction), [button element](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/block-elements/button-element), [block_actions payload](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/interaction-payloads/block_actions-payload), [unfurling links](https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/unfurling-links-in-messages), [installing with OAuth](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/installing-with-oauth), [users.lookupByEmail](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/users.lookupByEmail), [non-Marketplace rate limits changelog](https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/05/29/rate-limit-changes-for-non-marketplace-apps).

Microsoft: [send proactive messages](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/conversations/send-proactive-messages), [proactive install with Graph](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/graph-api/proactive-bots-and-messages/graph-proactive-bots-and-messages), [Adaptive Card actions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/task-modules-and-cards/cards/cards-actions), [Bot Connector authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bot-service/rest-api/bot-framework-rest-connector-authentication), [create an Azure Bot resource](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bot-service/abs-quickstart), [Graph get user](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/user-get?view=graph-rest-1.0), [publish overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/concepts/deploy-and-publish/apps-publish-overview), [Safe Links overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/safe-links-about).
